whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the Platform Data Architect exam?

personas.label: Data engineers
personas.description: You design data pipelines and migration processes and are responsible for data quality at scale on Salesforce.

personas.label: Enterprise architects
personas.description: You plan master data management, governance, and consistent data models across systems.

personas.label: Senior Salesforce developers
personas.description: You build integrations and data models and need to make sound choices for high-volume orgs.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Platform Data Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam spans data modeling, master data management, Salesforce data management, governance, large data volumes, and migration. Preparation means learning the published objectives and explaining the trade-offs among design choices.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
58% to pass, which is 35 correct answers out of 60.
Six weighted domains: data modeling, MDM, Salesforce data management, governance, large data volumes, and migration.
Exam fee: US$400; retake fee: US$200, plus applicable taxes. Prerequisite: none.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice explaining when a custom index, skinny table, or archive strategy fits. Also plan a parent-to-child migration and choose an MDM approach for records with conflicting values.

examFormat.heading: Platform Data Architect exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in person. Use the published objectives to guide preparation across all six domains.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Questions ask you to choose an architecture for a data model, migration, governance, or performance requirement. Be ready to compare options and explain the trade-offs.
bestWayToPass: Review the large data volume tools: Understand custom indexes, skinny tables, Async SOQL, Big Objects, and archiving, including each option’s limits.
Plan migrations carefully: Review parent-first loading, external ID upserts, Bulk API 2.0, and recovery plans for failed loads.
Compare MDM patterns: Study golden records, field survivorship, consolidation, and traceability.
Include governance: Consider privacy, classification, protection, stewardship, and enterprise policy in each design.

expertInsight: Use Salesforce's published exam objectives as the study scope. For large-data-volume and migration topics, compare design options against the stated access patterns, operational needs, and data-management requirements; do not assume one technique fits every scenario.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers Salesforce data modeling, data management, governance, migration, and large data volume design. Review when Big Objects, skinny tables, custom indexes, and MDM patterns fit. The guide also allows up to five unscored questions. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 58% pass mark, weighted towards Data Modeling/Database Design and Salesforce Data Management (25% each).

blocks.heading: Data Models, Relationships, and Big Objects
blocks.body: Choose standard or custom objects, external objects, and Big Objects based on the data and access pattern. Relationship types affect how records relate and how users access them. Big Objects support high-volume historical data, and queries are constrained by the configured index fields. Platform Events provide a schema-defined way to publish event messages. Evaluate each choice against the workload and published platform limits.

blocks.heading: Master Data Management and Duplicate Control
blocks.body: Master data management defines how systems identify important entities, resolve duplicates, and maintain trusted values. A golden record can be assembled using survivorship rules that select values by source trust or recency. Salesforce Matching Rules find records that may be duplicates; Duplicate Rules control what happens when a match is found. External IDs can support upserts and cross-system references. Design for traceability so teams can understand where values came from.

blocks.heading: Migration and Integration
blocks.body: Choose a migration method based on data volume, transformation needs, latency, and operations. Bulk API 2.0 supports asynchronous processing of large data loads and manages batches. External IDs support upsert and relationships across systems. Load parent records before dependent children when relationships require them. Plan validation, error handling, retries, and rollback or recovery before the migration begins.

blocks.heading: Data Quality and Governance
blocks.body: Governance sets expectations for data ownership, quality, privacy, classification, and protection. Validation Rules can reject values that fail business checks. Matching and Duplicate Rules help manage duplicate records, while field history features can support audit needs when configured. Select the controls that meet the organization’s policies and make ongoing stewardship part of the design.

blocks.heading: Large Data Volumes and Performance
blocks.body: At large scale, query selectivity, indexing, data growth, and archive strategy all affect performance. The query optimizer decides whether an available index is useful for a particular query. Custom indexes can support selective filters; skinny tables address certain query performance needs. Big Objects and external data options can support some historical or high-volume use cases. Follow current Salesforce guidance for the specific workload rather than assuming one tool fits every query.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Platform Data Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Start with the requirement and constraints: record relationships, data volume, latency, ownership, privacy, and recovery. Use them to narrow the architecture choices.

blocks.heading: Select the Relationship Type
blocks.body: Compare lookup, master-detail, self-referential, and external relationships. Consider required parentage, roll-up needs, deletion behavior, and access implications.

blocks.heading: Design for Growth
blocks.body: Review query selectivity, indexes, skinny tables, Big Objects, and archiving. Choose based on the access pattern and platform limits.

blocks.heading: Build Data Quality Controls
blocks.body: Use matching and duplicate controls to detect and handle repeats. Combine validation and stewardship processes with governance requirements.

blocks.heading: Plan the Migration
blocks.body: Use external IDs where needed, load parent records before dependent children, and select an API that matches volume and latency. Include validation, error handling, and recovery.

blocks.heading: Resolve Master Data
blocks.body: Compare registry, consolidation, and coexistence patterns. Define how a golden record is chosen, how conflicting attributes are resolved, and how source history is retained.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for Platform Data Architects
nextCertsAfter.intro: Continue with a Salesforce architecture credential or a role-focused data and integration specialization.

sampleQuestions.question: A custom object with tens of millions of rows is timing out because its query filters on a non-indexed field. What should the architect evaluate first?
options: Index the filter field when the query is selective
Increase the API request limit so the query can run longer
Move the object to a Big Object to remove query time limits
Enable a skinny table because it indexes every filtered field
sampleQuestions.explanation: A custom index may help the optimizer use a selective filter, provided the query and field meet platform requirements.
whyWrong: API request limits do not make an unselective database query faster.
Big Objects have query constraints and do not remove all time limits.
Skinny tables are not a general-purpose index for every filtered field.

sampleQuestions.question: Which set of concerns matters when designing for large data volumes?
options: Only the number of fields on the object
Governor limits, indexing, and query selectivity
Page layout complexity alone
The number of reports, without considering query patterns
sampleQuestions.explanation: Large-volume designs must account for platform limits, indexes, and how selective the queries will be.
whyWrong: This combines key performance and scale considerations.
Field count alone does not determine whether a large-volume query will perform well.
Page layouts do not address query selectivity or data volume.

sampleQuestions.question: A large Bulk API 2.0 load is causing row locks because many child records update the same parent. What should the team try?
options: Enable PK Chunking so updates to the shared parent run in parallel
Disable all validation rules for the whole migration
Group load rows by parent lookup
Reduce every batch to one record
sampleQuestions.explanation: Grouping records by parent can help organize processing and reduce concurrent updates to the same parent, subject to the load design.
whyWrong: PK Chunking splits work by record ranges and may not solve contention on a shared parent.
This helps keep related updates together and can reduce locking contention.
Disabling every validation rule may undermine data quality and does not directly resolve parent locks.

sampleQuestions.question: A child record must always have a parent, and it should inherit key access and lifecycle behavior from that parent. Which relationship is appropriate?
options: Lookup
External lookup
Indirect lookup
Master-detail
sampleQuestions.explanation: A master-detail relationship requires a parent and ties key access and lifecycle behavior to that parent.
whyWrong: A lookup can allow a child record to exist without a parent.
This relationship type fits the required parent dependency.
External and indirect lookups link to external records rather than enforcing this standard parent relationship.

sampleQuestions.question: What does an archiving strategy address?
options: Move historical data off-platform and retain required access
Keeping a second backup in the same object
Deleting historical data immediately without review
Exporting records once without defining future retrieval
sampleQuestions.explanation: Archiving moves older data from active storage while considering how it may need to be accessed later.
whyWrong: A backup alone does not reduce active data volume or define archive access.
Immediate deletion may violate retention or business needs.
A one-time export does not define ongoing retention or retrieval.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a Salesforce Big Object designed to support?
options: A standard CRM record with a large set of page layouts
High-volume, append-oriented historical data
A report type for joined dashboard data
A dashboard with very many widgets
sampleQuestions.explanation: Big Objects support large volumes of data, commonly for historical or archival use cases.
whyWrong: Big Objects are not standard CRM objects configured with page layouts.
Report types are a separate reporting feature.
Dashboard size is unrelated to Big Objects.

sampleQuestions.question: Which indexing approach can improve a selective SOQL query?
options: Avoid indexes on fields used in filters
Use suitable indexes to support selective filtered queries
Index filtered fields selectively
Index formula fields only
sampleQuestions.explanation: Standard and custom indexes can help when the query filters are selective and the index is appropriate.
whyWrong: Avoiding indexes may leave a selective query without useful access paths.
This is the appropriate approach, subject to selectivity and platform guidance.
Indexing every field is not supported or useful as a general strategy.

sampleQuestions.question: Two source systems contain the same customer but disagree on the phone number. How should an MDM design choose the golden record value?
options: Keep the value from whichever system was loaded first
Store both values permanently without selecting a trusted value
Discard both values and ask the customer to re-enter them
Apply a survivorship rule using source trust or recency
sampleQuestions.explanation: A survivorship rule defines which source value wins, using criteria such as source trust or most recent update.
whyWrong: Load order is not a reliable business rule for choosing an attribute.
Keeping both values without a resolution policy does not establish a usable golden record.
Requiring re-entry discards available source data and does not define MDM behavior.

sampleQuestions.question: Which relationship can allow a child record to exist without a parent record?
options: Lookup
A junction record may use two parent relationships
A junction object commonly links two records through relationships
Indirect lookup
sampleQuestions.explanation: A lookup relationship can be optional, allowing the child record to exist without a linked parent.
whyWrong: Master-detail requires a parent record.
A junction object commonly uses master-detail relationships and is not the general answer here.
Indirect lookup links external records and does not describe the standard optional parent relationship.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a soft-delete approach?
options: Permanently erase data immediately
Mark deleted but retain for recovery or compliance
Export records without changing their status
Move records to an archive and remove all references
sampleQuestions.explanation: Soft deletion marks records as deleted while retaining them for a defined recovery or retention period.
whyWrong: Permanent erasure is a hard delete, not a soft delete.
Exporting data does not change its deletion status.
Archiving may be part of retention but is not the definition of soft delete.

sampleQuestions.question: Which synchronous SOQL query limit applies to Apex transactions?
options: There is no per-transaction SOQL query limit
Unlimited queries when using Bulk API
100 SOQL queries per transaction
50 SOQL queries per transaction
sampleQuestions.explanation: A synchronous Apex transaction is subject to a limit of 100 SOQL queries.
whyWrong: Salesforce enforces a per-transaction query limit.
Bulk API does not remove Apex transaction governor limits.
The synchronous limit is not 50 queries.

sampleQuestions.question: What problem does master data management address?
options: Reporting and dashboard layout
Archiving old records only
Migrating data without resolving duplicates
Deduplicate and improve data quality
sampleQuestions.explanation: MDM establishes trusted data through practices such as deduplication, survivorship, and ongoing quality management.
whyWrong: Reporting layout is not the core purpose of MDM.
Archiving may support data management but does not establish trusted master records.
Migration alone does not resolve duplicate or conflicting data.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Salesforce data store is suited to high-volume append-oriented historical data?
options: A standard CRM object for ordinary transactional records
A Big Object is intended for very high volumes of historical data
A custom object with triggers on every insert
An external object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Big Objects are designed for very large volumes of data, including append-oriented historical data.
whyWrong: Standard objects are not designed specifically for this high-volume archive pattern.
Custom triggers add processing and do not make a custom object a Big Object.
External objects expose data stored outside Salesforce rather than storing it in a Big Object.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a benefit of using an external object?
options: It replaces all custom objects in the org
Query external records without copying them
It archives Salesforce records automatically
It creates reports without requiring a data source
sampleQuestions.explanation: External objects let users work with data stored outside Salesforce without replicating it into the org.
whyWrong: External objects complement rather than replace custom objects.
Archiving Salesforce records requires a separate archive design.
Reports still require an underlying data source.

sampleQuestions.question: Which design choice helps prepare for growth in data volume?
options: Ignore platform limits until performance declines
Rely only on backups
Archive data, add useful indexes, and keep queries selective
Export all data without defining retrieval needs
sampleQuestions.explanation: Archiving and selective query design help manage growth while preserving the access the business needs.
whyWrong: Waiting until a problem appears can leave little time to correct architecture.
Backups do not reduce active data volume or improve query selectivity.
Exports without a retrieval plan do not form a complete data strategy.
